passages.t: The covenant broken, and do not pray for them
passages.happening:
God tells Jeremiah to proclaim the words of the covenant to Judah and Jerusalem (verse 2). ‘Cursed is the man who does not obey the words of this covenant’ (verse 3), the covenant God gave when he brought their fathers out of the iron furnace of Egypt (verse 4). Jeremiah answers, ‘Amen, LORD’ (verse 5).

God warned their fathers again and again to obey, ‘Yet they would not obey or incline their ears’ (verse 8), so the curses of the covenant came on them. Now there is a conspiracy among the people of Judah: they have gone back to the sins of their fathers and followed other gods (verses 9 and 10). God will bring a disaster they cannot escape. They will cry out, and he will not listen (verse 11). They will cry to the gods they burned incense to, and those gods will not save them (verse 12). Judah's gods are as many as its cities (verse 13).

‘As for you, do not pray for these people’ (verse 14). What right has God's beloved in his house, after so many evil schemes (verse 15)? God once called them ‘a flourishing olive tree, beautiful with well-formed fruit’ (verse 16), but now he will set it on fire.
passages.hearers:
Many interpreters connect this chapter's covenant language with King Josiah's reform. In 622 BC a book of the law was found in the temple, and the king led the people in renewing the covenant and cleared away the shrines of Baal. Most scholars identify that book with Deuteronomy or a form of it.

A covenant in the ancient world was a binding agreement, often between a great king and a lesser people, sealed with an oath and backed by promises for loyalty and curses for betrayal. Israel's covenant with the LORD follows that pattern. Verse 3 echoes Deuteronomy 27, where the people answered each curse with Amen. Jeremiah says Amen too.

The olive tree was one of the glories of the land, living for centuries and bearing fruit year after year. God had planted Israel like that. Now the tree will burn.
passages.later: In Deuteronomy the people answered the curses with ‘Amen’ (Deuteronomy 27:26). A psalm says, ‘I am like an olive tree flourishing in the house of God’ (Psalm 52:8).
passages.hard:
Why would God forbid Jeremiah to pray for the people?

It is one of the hardest lines in the book, and it comes three times (7:16; 11:14; 14:11). It does not mean prayer is useless or that God has stopped caring; the next chapters show God grieving over his people. The sense is that the verdict on this generation has been reached, and intercession will not turn away the coming disaster, much as a doctor may say treatment can no longer prevent what is coming. Some interpreters also note that the people's own prayers in verse 11 were not repentance but panic, using God as one more god to call on in a crisis.

Jeremiah in fact keeps praying for them in chapter 14, and God answers him honestly. The command is less a wall than a sign of how late the hour is. It is not a word for any reader to stop praying for anyone.
passages.asks: Jeremiah said Amen to the covenant's curses. Ask whether you take God's warnings as seriously as his promises. And ask whether your own prayers in trouble are a turning to God, or only a cry for rescue.

passages.t: A lamb led to slaughter: the plot at Anathoth
passages.happening:
‘And the LORD informed me, so I knew. Then You showed me their deeds’ (verse 18). Jeremiah had been like a gentle lamb led to slaughter, not knowing that they were plotting to cut him off from the land of the living, so that his name would be remembered no more (verse 19).

‘O LORD of Hosts, who judges righteously, who examines the heart and mind, let me see Your vengeance upon them, for to You I have committed my cause’ (verse 20).

God answers concerning the men of Anathoth, who are seeking Jeremiah's life and telling him not to prophesy in the LORD's name (verse 21). He will punish them. Their young men will die by the sword and their children by famine (verse 22). There will be no remnant for them in the year of their punishment (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Anathoth was a town of priests in Benjamin, a few miles from Jerusalem, and Jeremiah's birthplace. The men plotting to kill him were his own townspeople, and the next chapter says his own family was among them.

This is the first of Jeremiah's private prayers, his confessions. He does not take revenge himself. He hands his cause to the God who judges righteously and sees the heart.

The lamb led to slaughter is a picture of trust that did not see danger coming. Isaiah uses the same picture of the Servant.
passages.later: Isaiah says of the Servant, ‘He was led like a lamb to the slaughter’ (Isaiah 53:7). Paul tells believers not to avenge themselves but to ‘leave room for God’s wrath’ (Romans 12:19).
passages.hard:
Jeremiah asks to see God's vengeance, and God says the children of Anathoth will die by famine. How should a reader take that?

Jeremiah's prayer hands his enemies to God rather than taking revenge himself, and the Bible keeps such prayers as honest cries, not as patterns for how to treat enemies. The judgment on Anathoth falls in the coming siege and famine, when all Judah suffered. It is not a teaching that children are punished for their parents, and it gives no warrant to read any child's suffering as deserved. Ezra 2 later lists men of Anathoth among those who came home, a sign that the last word was not destruction.
passages.asks: Jeremiah found that his own people were plotting against him. Ask whether you have been hurt by those closest to you, and what you have done with it. And ask whether you could commit your cause to God instead of fighting for it yourself.
